source.title: Principal Components Bias in Over-parameterized Linear Models, and its Manifestation in Deep Neural Networks

record.tranche_reason: The study compares learning curves for real and shuffled labels in deep linear networks, and reports a convergence-rate difference; its own results therefore bear on V2. It does not reproduce the random-label fitting protocol sufficiently to assess the full V1 outcome.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2017) for networks learning any assignment; that cited result is not recorded as a row. Figure 9 reports the study's own real-versus-shuffled-label learning curves. Figure 10 uses labels modified to make datasets linearly separable, not completely random labelings.
record.test_reason: Section 6 and Figure 9 directly compare convergence with original and shuffled labels in two-layer linear networks, before and after whitening. These results test the label-dependent slowdown component of V2, but do not establish its small constant-factor training-time claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors find slower convergence with shuffled labels in deep linear networks and identical rates after whitening, attributing this difference to PC-bias. Their nonlinear experiments provide complementary evidence using deliberately separable label constructions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses real versus fully shuffled labels and compares learning curves, but studies linear networks and does not report the original claim's full training-error and test-error outcomes or a sweep over corruption levels.
record.method_sensitivity: The label-related convergence difference is present for natural images and absent after ZCA whitening.

fits_no_version.finding: In Figure 10, nonlinear st-VGG networks learn faster when fewer leading principal components suffice for separation, with little qualitative difference between the two label constructions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Convergence depends on which principal components carry discriminative information, even when labels are constructed from different starting assignments. These labels are modified to ensure linear separability and are not completely random.

record.problems: For the random-label comparison, the reported learning curves are figure-only; exact convergence times and endpoints are not stated. Only fully shuffled labels are compared with original labels, and only in deep linear networks.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results omitted. Figure 10 uses labels adjusted to make datasets linearly separable, rather than a sweep over random-label corruption, so it is not a row for the listed versions.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and fitting with unchanged training hyperparameters are not established.

A small constant-factor increase in time to successful fitting and the trend across intermediate corruption fractions are not measured. Hyperparameters were grid-searched in each experimental setup, so a fixed-hyperparameter comparison is not established.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across increasing fractions of corrupted labels.
Whether regularization prevents random-label fitting, and whether removing regularization harms true-label generalization. Using dropout alone does not establish either result.
Whether shared real-data patterns are fitted before noisy labels are memorized. Separate original-versus-shuffled learning curves do not isolate these phases within training on noisy labels.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 9's numerical curves are unavailable in the supplied text; the qualitative comparisons are explicit. Neither slower convergence nor identical convergence rates establishes zero-error random-label fitting.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report whether its networks reach zero or near-zero training error with completely random labels, or test error at chance.
It compares true labels with fully shuffled labels, but does not test a small constant-factor time cost or convergence across intermediate fractions of corrupted labels.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input conditions.
No sweep over fractions of randomly corrupted labels or corresponding test-error measurements.
No test of regularization or augmentation effects on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
No measurement of whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

rows.note: The text states that the networks converge slower with random labels. The curves are shown only in the figure; exact rates and endpoints are not stated. Aggregate result for 10 networks.
rows.check: The reported slowdown is correctly recorded. Specify the cats-and-dogs dataset and original versus shuffled label conditions, rather than original labels alone. statements.correction: R1: slower convergence with shuffled labels before whitening. R2: identical convergence rates after whitening. Both concern label-dependent slowdown.
statements.problem: The whitening finding is accurate, but R1 and R2 concern the same slowdown component of V2 under different preprocessing conditions; different clauses do not explain their different states.
